passages.text: My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism.
passages.original: Ἀδελφοί μου μὴ ἐν προσωπολημψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίστιν τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τῆς δόξης
passages.objections:
I think it's only natural to treat the wealthy with more respect—they can help the church more than the poor ever could.
Why should I bother being kind to someone who can't offer me anything in return?
Isn't it just common sense to give the best seats to the most important people?
If someone looks successful, doesn't that mean God has blessed them more?
I don't see the harm in favoring those who dress well; it makes our gatherings look more respectable.
Shouldn't we focus our attention on people who have influence and power?
Why waste time on the needy when they can't contribute much to our community?
Isn't it okay to judge people by their appearance? After all, first impressions matter.
If someone is poor, maybe it's because they haven't worked hard enough, so why should I treat them the same?
Does it really matter if I treat my friends better than strangers?

passages.text: Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in.
passages.original: Ἐὰν γὰρ εἰσέλθῃ εἰς συναγωγὴν ὑμῶν ἀνὴρ χρυσοδακτύλιος ἐν ἐσθῆτι λαμπρᾷ εἰσέλθῃ δὲ καὶ πτωχὸς ἐν ῥυπαρᾷ ἐσθῆτι
passages.objections:
We should give the best seat to the man who looks wealthy because he probably deserves it.
It's only natural to treat someone better if they look important or rich.
People in shabby clothes shouldn't expect the same respect as those who dress well.
If someone can't afford nice clothes, maybe they don't belong here.
We should focus our attention on those who can help the church financially.
The poor man should be grateful just to be allowed in at all.
It's not wrong to honor those who are successful in the world.
Why should we treat everyone the same when some people clearly have more to offer?
If someone looks poor, they probably don't have much faith or blessing.
We need to impress the wealthy visitors so they keep coming back.

passages.text: If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
passages.original: ἐπιβλέψητε δὲ ἐπὶ τὸν φοροῦντα τὴν ἐσθῆτα τὴν λαμπρὰν καὶ εἴπητε Σὺ κάθου ὧδε καλῶς καὶ τῷ πτωχῷ εἴπητε Σὺ στῆθι ἐκεῖ ἢ Κάθου ὑπὸ τὸ ὑποπόδιόν μου καὶ οὐ διεκρίθητε ἐν ἑαυτοῖς καὶ ἐγένεσθε κριταὶ διαλογισμῶν πονηρῶν
passages.objections:
We should give the best seats to the wealthy because they can help our church more.
It’s only natural to treat important-looking people better than those who look poor.
If someone is dressed nicely, they probably deserve more respect than someone in shabby clothes.
I don’t see any harm in making the poor stand while the rich sit comfortably.
People with money should get special treatment since they contribute more.
It’s just common sense to honor those who appear successful.
The poor should be grateful just to be allowed in at all.
We need to impress the rich so they’ll want to join us.
It’s not wrong to judge people by their appearance; it helps us know who’s valuable.
If someone looks poor, they probably haven’t worked as hard as the rich folks.

passages.text: Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him?
passages.original: Ἀκούσατε ἀδελφοί μου ἀγαπητοί οὐχ ὁ Θεὸς ἐξελέξατο τοὺς πτωχοὺς τῷ κόσμῳ πλουσίους ἐν πίστει καὶ κληρονόμους τῆς βασιλείας ἧς ἐπηγγείλατο τοῖς ἀγαπῶσιν αὐτόν
passages.objections:
I just don’t see how someone poor could ever be important to God.
If you don’t have wealth, you must not be blessed or favored.
Only those with money and status can really make a difference in God’s kingdom.
Why would God care about people who have nothing to offer?
Faith is nice, but it’s riches and power that really matter in this world.
The poor are probably being punished for something—they can’t be chosen by God.
If someone is struggling, it means God hasn’t picked them for anything special.
Surely God’s promises are for those who have proven themselves with success.
I think only the wealthy can truly inherit anything valuable from God.
Why should we pay attention to the poor when they have so little influence?

passages.text: But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court?
passages.original: ὑμεῖς δὲ ἠτιμάσατε τὸν πτωχόν οὐχ οἱ πλούσιοι καταδυναστεύουσιν ὑμῶν καὶ αὐτοὶ ἕλκουσιν ὑμᾶς εἰς κριτήρια
passages.objections:
Why should we care about the poor? The rich are the ones who really matter in our community.
I think it’s better to honor those with wealth—they have the power to help us.
The poor probably did something to deserve their situation, so why should we respect them?
If we treat the rich well, maybe they’ll protect us or give us favors.
Isn’t it just practical to side with those who have influence and money?
The poor can’t do anything for us, so why bother giving them any special attention?
We should focus on pleasing the wealthy, since they set the rules around here.
I don’t see any harm in ignoring the poor—they’re used to it anyway.
If we honor the rich, maybe they’ll stop making life hard for us.
It’s only natural to look up to those who have more than we do.

passages.text: Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?
passages.original: οὐκ αὐτοὶ βλασφημοῦσιν τὸ καλὸν ὄνομα τὸ ἐπικληθὲν ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς
passages.objections:
I don’t see any harm in siding with the wealthy; they’re the ones who help our community the most.
The rich must be more blessed by God, so we should honor them above others.
It’s only the poor who cause trouble for believers, not the rich.
Those with power and money always respect our faith and traditions.
Wealthy people never speak badly about what we believe.
If someone is successful, that means they must be righteous and on our side.
I’ve never heard anyone with influence insult our faith, so it can’t be a problem.
Why would the rich ever oppose us? They have everything they need.
It’s only outsiders and strangers who mock our beliefs, not those in high places.
People with status and money always support the good name we carry.

passages.text: If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well.
passages.original: Εἰ μέντοι νόμον τελεῖτε βασιλικὸν κατὰ τὴν γραφήν Ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν καλῶς ποιεῖτε
passages.objections:
Why should I care about anyone but myself? 
I don’t see why I should treat others the same way I want to be treated.
Some people just don’t deserve kindness from me.
It’s enough to just follow the rules; I don’t need to actually love anyone.
I can pick and choose who I’m nice to, right?
Helping others isn’t my responsibility.
If someone wrongs me, I don’t have to treat them well.
Loving my neighbor is just a suggestion, not something I have to do.
I’m only supposed to look out for my own interests.
People should earn my respect before I treat them well.

passages.text: But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
passages.original: εἰ δὲ προσωπολημπτεῖτε ἁμαρτίαν ἐργάζεσθε ἐλεγχόμενοι ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου ὡς παραβάται
passages.objections:
I don’t see anything wrong with treating my rich friends better than the poor ones.
It’s not a big deal if I give special treatment to people I like more.
Surely God doesn’t care if I favor my own family over strangers.
I can’t help it if I respect people with more influence in the community.
Isn’t it normal to treat important guests better than others?
I don’t think it’s a sin to prefer those who can help me in return.
Why should I treat everyone the same when some people deserve more honor?
It’s just practical to be nicer to those who have power or wealth.
I’m not hurting anyone by ignoring people who don’t fit in.
God understands if I look out for my own kind first.

passages.text: Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it.
passages.original: Ὅστις γὰρ ὅλον τὸν νόμον τηρήσῃ πταίσῃ δὲ ἐν ἑνί γέγονεν πάντων ἔνοχος
passages.objections:
I’ve done almost everything right, so surely one little mistake doesn’t matter that much.
If I avoid the big sins, the small ones can’t really count against me, can they?
As long as I follow most of the rules, I’m still a good person in God’s eyes.
Nobody’s perfect, so God must overlook the few times I mess up.
I only broke one commandment, so I’m not really a lawbreaker.
If I keep the important parts of the law, the rest isn’t as serious.
I can make up for my mistakes by doing extra good deeds.
God grades on a curve, so as long as I’m better than most, I’m fine.
It’s impossible to keep every rule, so God can’t expect that from us.
One slip-up can’t possibly ruin all the good I’ve done.

passages.text: For He who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker.
passages.original: ὁ γὰρ εἰπών Μὴ μοιχεύσῃς εἶπεν καί Μὴ φονεύσῃς εἰ δὲ οὐ μοιχεύεις φονεύεις δέ γέγονας παραβάτης νόμου
passages.objections:
I haven’t broken all the rules, just one, so I’m still a good person, right?
As long as I avoid the really bad sins, the smaller ones don’t matter much.
If I keep most of the commandments, God will overlook the ones I break.
It’s okay if I mess up in one area, because I’m faithful in everything else.
I only need to follow the commandments that are most important to me.
Breaking one law isn’t the same as being a lawbreaker, is it?
I can pick and choose which rules to follow and still be righteous.
God won’t judge me harshly if I only slip up once.
As long as I don’t commit the worst sins, I’m not really guilty.
If I avoid adultery, it doesn’t matter if I do something else wrong.

passages.text: Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom.
passages.original: Οὕτως λαλεῖτε καὶ οὕτως ποιεῖτε ὡς διὰ νόμου ἐλευθερίας μέλλοντες κρίνεσθαι
passages.objections:
Why should I worry about how I treat others if I’m already forgiven?
I don’t think my words really matter as long as I believe the right things.
Isn’t it enough to just follow the rules without caring about people?
Why should I act differently just because I’m a Christian?
I can say whatever I want; it’s my actions that count, not my speech.
If I’m saved by grace, why bother trying to live any differently?
I don’t need to think about judgment since I’m already free.
It doesn’t matter how I speak to others; God only looks at my heart.
Why should I be held to a higher standard than everyone else?
As long as I avoid the big sins, the rest doesn’t really matter.

passages.text: For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
passages.original: ἡ γὰρ κρίσις ἀνέλεος τῷ μὴ ποιήσαντι ἔλεος κατακαυχᾶται ἔλεος κρίσεως
passages.objections:
I don’t have to forgive others if they’ve wronged me too badly.
People who mess up deserve to be punished, not shown kindness.
Why should I help someone who never helped me?
Mercy is for the weak; justice means giving people what they deserve.
If I’m strict and harsh with others, that’s just being fair.
I can judge others harshly because I follow all the rules myself.
There’s no point in being merciful; it just lets people take advantage of you.
I don’t need to show compassion to those who don’t deserve it.
It’s better to be tough and unforgiving so people learn their lesson.

passages.text: What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him?
passages.original: Τί τὸ ὄφελος ἀδελφοί μου ἐὰν πίστιν λέγῃ τις ἔχειν ἔργα δὲ μὴ ἔχῃ μὴ δύναται ἡ πίστις σῶσαι αὐτόν
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything special as long as I say I believe.
Isn’t it enough just to have faith in my heart, even if I never help anyone?
Why should I bother with good works if I already trust in God?
I can just talk about my faith and that’s all that matters.
Helping others isn’t really necessary for my salvation, is it?
As long as I pray and believe, my actions don’t matter.
Faith is just about what I think, not what I do.
I don’t need to prove my faith by doing anything for others.
Isn’t faith just a private thing between me and God?
Why should I worry about the needs of others if I believe?

passages.text: Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food.
passages.original: ἐὰν ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἀδελφὴ γυμνοὶ ὑπάρχωσιν καὶ λειπόμενοι τῆς ἐφημέρου τροφῆς
passages.objections:
If someone is struggling, it's not really my responsibility to help them.
I think wishing someone well is enough; I don't need to actually do anything.
As long as I have good intentions, it doesn't matter if I don't provide for their needs.
People should just pray for help instead of expecting others to step in.
If I just tell them to stay strong, that's all the encouragement they need.
God will take care of them, so I don't have to get involved.
It's not my fault if someone is hungry or cold; they should figure it out themselves.
I don't have to give anything; just saying kind words is enough.
Helping others is optional, not something I need to worry about.
My faith is personal, so I don't need to show it by helping others.

passages.text: If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that?
passages.original: εἴπῃ δέ τις αὐτοῖς ἐξ ὑμῶν Ὑπάγετε ἐν εἰρήνῃ θερμαίνεσθε καὶ χορτάζεσθε μὴ δῶτε δὲ αὐτοῖς τὰ ἐπιτήδεια τοῦ σώματος τί τὸ ὄφελος
passages.objections:
I don’t need to actually help the poor as long as I wish them well in my heart.
Just saying a kind word is enough; I don’t have to give anything.
It’s not my responsibility if someone is hungry or cold—I can just pray for them.
As long as I have good intentions, I don’t need to take action.
God only cares about my words, not what I do for others.
If I tell someone to stay warm and fed, that’s all that matters.
Helping with physical needs isn’t as important as spiritual encouragement.
I can’t really make a difference, so why bother giving anything?
It’s enough to send people away with a blessing instead of meeting their needs.

passages.text: So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.
passages.original: οὕτως καὶ ἡ πίστις ἐὰν μὴ ἔχῃ ἔργα νεκρά ἐστιν καθ’ ἑαυτήν
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything special for others as long as I believe in my heart.
Isn’t it enough just to say I have faith and not worry about helping anyone?
Why should I bother with good deeds if I already trust in God?
My beliefs are private, so my actions don’t really matter.
As long as I pray and believe, I don’t have to get involved in anyone’s troubles.
Faith is just about what I think, not what I do.
I can ignore people in need because my faith alone will save me.
Helping others isn’t necessary if I have strong faith.
God only cares about what’s inside, not what I actually do.
I don’t need to prove my faith to anyone by doing good works.

passages.text: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have deeds.” Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds.
passages.original: Ἀλλ’ ἐρεῖ τις Σὺ πίστιν ἔχεις κἀγὼ ἔργα ἔχω δεῖξόν μοι τὴν πίστιν σου χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων κἀγώ σοι δείξω ἐκ τῶν ἔργων μου τὴν πίστιν
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything special to prove I have faith—believing is enough.
Why should I bother helping others if I already trust in God?
Isn’t it possible to have real faith without ever showing it?
My actions don’t matter as long as I believe in my heart.
No one can see my faith, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t real.
I can just keep my faith private and not worry about what I do.
Faith and good deeds are totally separate; one doesn’t need the other.
As long as I say I believe, I don’t have to do anything else.
People can’t judge my faith by what I do or don’t do.
It’s not important to show my faith to anyone else.

passages.text: You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder.
passages.original: σὺ πιστεύεις ὅτι εἷς ἐστιν ὁ Θεός καλῶς ποιεῖς καὶ τὰ δαιμόνια πιστεύουσιν καὶ φρίσσουσιν
passages.objections:
I believe in God, so that’s all I need to be right with Him.
Isn’t it enough just to know that God exists?
As long as I say I believe, nothing else really matters, right?
Believing in God is the only thing required; actions don’t count.
I don’t need to do anything else if I already accept that there’s one God.
Just having faith in my mind is enough for salvation.
If I acknowledge God, I’m already better than most people.
Why should I worry about anything else if I believe in the one true God?
Isn’t belief alone what sets me apart from everyone else?
I don’t need to change how I live, as long as I believe in God.

passages.text: O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?
passages.original: Θέλεις δὲ γνῶναι ὦ ἄνθρωπε κενέ ὅτι ἡ πίστις χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων ἀργή ἐστιν
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything special to prove I have faith—believing is enough.
Why should I bother helping others if I already trust in God?
Isn’t it enough just to say I believe, even if my life doesn’t change?
Actions don’t matter as long as my heart is in the right place.
I can just keep my faith private and not worry about what I do.
God only cares about what I believe, not what I actually do.
I don’t need to show my faith to anyone; it’s between me and God.
As long as I believe, I don’t have to worry about doing good things.
Faith is just about what I think, not about how I live.
Deeds are for people who want to look good, not for real believers like me.

passages.text: Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?
passages.original: Ἀβραὰμ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη ἀνενέγκας Ἰσαὰκ τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον
passages.objections:
I don’t think actions matter as long as you believe in your heart.
Isn’t faith enough on its own? Why would anyone need to do anything more?
God only cares about what we say we believe, not what we actually do.
If I just say I trust God, that should be all He wants from me.
Why would God expect us to prove our faith with difficult choices?
Obedience doesn’t really show faith; it’s just following rules.
I can have a strong faith without ever having to act on it.
Isn’t it unfair for God to ask for such a big sacrifice to prove faith?
Actions are just for show; they don’t really mean anything to God.
If Abraham already believed, why did he have to do anything else?

passages.text: You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did.
passages.original: βλέπεις ὅτι ἡ πίστις συνήργει τοῖς ἔργοις αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκ τῶν ἔργων ἡ πίστις ἐτελειώθη
passages.objections:
I don’t see why I need to do anything if I already believe in God.
Isn’t faith just about what’s in your heart, not what you do?
Why should my actions matter if I trust God?
Can’t I just say I have faith and leave it at that?
Isn’t believing enough, even if I never help anyone?
Why bother with good deeds if faith alone saves me?
Doesn’t God only care about my beliefs, not my behavior?
If I have faith, why do I need to prove it with works?
Aren’t actions pointless if I already have faith?
Isn’t it possible to have perfect faith without ever doing anything?

passages.text: And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.
passages.original: καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα Ἐπίστευσεν δὲ Ἀβραὰμ τῷ Θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην καὶ φίλος Θεοῦ ἐκλήθη
passages.objections:
I don’t think just believing in God is enough to make someone right with Him.
How could someone be called God’s friend just because they trust Him?
Isn’t it impossible for anyone to be considered righteous in God’s eyes?
Faith alone can’t really change a person’s standing before God, can it?
Why would God care about someone’s belief more than their actions?
I doubt that trusting God could ever fulfill what the Scriptures require.
You have to do a lot of good deeds before God would ever accept you.
God only calls prophets and holy people His friends, not ordinary believers.
There’s no way someone like Abraham could be counted righteous just by faith.
Being close to God must take years of perfect living, not just believing.

passages.text: As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone.
passages.original: ὁρᾶτε ὅτι ἐξ ἔργων δικαιοῦται ἄνθρωπος καὶ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μόνον
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything good as long as I believe in my heart.
Faith is all that matters; my actions don’t count for anything.
Why bother helping others if I already trust in God?
I can just say I believe and never change how I live.
It doesn’t matter if I ignore people in need, as long as I have faith.
God only cares about what I believe, not what I do.
I can live however I want because my faith alone saves me.
There’s no point in trying to do good works if I already have faith.
My actions can’t possibly affect my standing with God.
Obeying God’s commands isn’t necessary if I just believe.

passages.text: In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route?
passages.original: Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη οὐκ ἐξ ἔργων ἐδικαιώθη ὑποδεξαμένη τοὺς ἀγγέλους καὶ ἑτέρᾳ ὁδῷ ἐκβαλοῦσα
passages.objections:
There's no way someone with a past like Rahab's could ever be right with God.
God only cares about people who have always lived good, respectable lives.
Actions don't matter at all if you just say you believe.
God would never use someone with such a bad reputation for His purposes.
Once you've sinned as much as Rahab, there's no coming back.
Faith alone is enough, so what you do doesn't make any difference.
People from outside God's chosen people can't be accepted, no matter what they do.
God only looks at your background, not your choices or actions.
If you've made big mistakes, God won't ever forgive or use you.
Helping others or doing good deeds can't change your standing with God.

passages.text: As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.
passages.original: ὥσπερ γὰρ τὸ σῶμα χωρὶς πνεύματος νεκρόν ἐστιν οὕτως καὶ ἡ πίστις χωρὶς ἔργων νεκρά ἐστιν
passages.objections:
I don’t need to do anything good as long as I believe in my heart.
Isn’t it enough to just say I have faith and not worry about my actions?
Why should I bother helping others if I already trust in God?
My faith is private, so what I do doesn’t really matter.
I can just sit back and believe; God doesn’t care about my works.
As long as I pray and believe, I don’t need to change how I live.
Good deeds are for show-offs; faith alone is all that counts.
Actions don’t prove anything about my relationship with God.
I don’t need to serve others to be right with God, just believe.
It’s impossible for faith to be dead, even if I never do anything with it.
